front: What does well-founded mean?
back: There are no infinite descending chains, or equivalently every nonempty set has a minimal element under the relation.

front: What is a well-founded relation used for?
back: Induction and recursion over structures more general than natural numbers.

front: What is well-founded induction?
back: To prove a property for `x`, assume it for all smaller predecessors of `x`, then prove it for `x`.

front: What is the proof shape of well-founded induction?
back: `∀ x, (∀ y, y ≺ x → P y) → P x` implies `∀ x, P x`.

front: How does well-founded induction differ from ordinary induction?
back: The induction step may use all smaller/predecessor cases, not only one immediate predecessor.

front: What is a descending chain?
back: A sequence `x₀, x₁, x₂, ...` where each next element is strictly smaller than the previous one.

front: Why does an infinite descending chain violate well-foundedness?
back: It prevents reaching a minimal base case.

front: What is a minimal element?
back: An element with no strictly smaller element in the set.

front: What is accessibility?
back: An element is accessible if all its predecessors are accessible; well-foundedness says every element is accessible.

front: What is structural recursion?
back: Recursion justified because recursive calls are made on structurally smaller data.

front: What is measure-based recursion?
back: Recursion justified by mapping data to a well-founded measure, often natural numbers.

front: What does well-defined mean?
back: A definition gives a unique, unambiguous value independent of presentation or choices.

front: When is well-definedness an issue?
back: When objects have multiple names, representatives, witnesses, or construction choices.

front: Why do quotient constructions require well-definedness proofs?
back: The output must not depend on which representative of an equivalence class is chosen.

front: What is the standard quotient-operation well-definedness shape?
back: If `a ~ a'` and `b ~ b'`, then `op a b ~ op a' b'`.

front: What is a representative?
back: A chosen object standing for an equivalence class.

front: Why are representatives dangerous?
back: Different representatives can denote the same equivalence class.

front: What does it mean for a function on representatives to descend to a quotient?
back: Equivalent representatives are sent to equivalent outputs.

front: What is the difference between existence and well-definedness?
back: Existence says some object/value is available; well-definedness says the result is unique or independent of choices.

front: What is the difference between uniqueness and well-definedness?
back: Uniqueness often proves there is only one possible value; well-definedness often proves all choices produce the same value or equivalent values.

front: What is the proof pattern for well-definedness?
back: Assume two valid choices or equivalent representatives, then prove their outputs agree.

front: Why is rational addition by pairs a well-definedness problem?
back: The same rational can be represented by many integer pairs, so addition must respect the equivalence relation.

front: Why is defining a function by "choose an element" risky?
back: Without uniqueness or choice data, different choices may produce different outputs.

front: Why is inverse construction often noncomputable?
back: It may rely on existence/uniqueness or choice rather than an explicit algorithm.

front: What theorem usually follows a noncomputable choice definition?
back: A correctness theorem showing the chosen object satisfies the desired property.

front: What is a "respects equivalence" theorem?
back: A theorem saying equivalent inputs produce equivalent outputs.

front: How does congruence relate to well-definedness?
back: Congruence is the compatibility property that often proves quotient definitions are well-defined.

front: What is a failure mode for well-definedness?
back: Giving a formula on representatives but not proving it respects the equivalence relation.

front: What is a failure mode for well-foundedness?
back: Defining recursion where recursive calls are not demonstrably smaller.

front: What Lean tactic often starts a well-definedness proof?
back: `intro` or `rintro` to bring representatives and equivalence hypotheses into context.

front: What Lean tactic often unpacks representative data?
back: `rcases`.

front: What Lean tool helps with chains of equality or equivalence?
back: `calc`.

front: What Lean command names an intermediate compatibility fact?
back: `have`.

front: When should you unfold in well-definedness proofs?
back: When the equivalence relation or operation definition must be exposed to prove compatibility.

front: When should you avoid unfolding?
back: When named lemmas already state the needed compatibility or equivalence behavior.

front: What should a well-definedness theorem name communicate?
back: Which operation or construction is independent of which choices.

front: What should a well-foundedness theorem name communicate?
back: Which relation or measure justifies induction/recursion.

front: What is the safe construction workflow?
back: Define relation, prove equivalence/well-foundedness as needed, prove compatibility/well-definedness, then expose the final operation.
